markets.name: Nassau County
markets.tagline: Florida's northeast corner, where I-95, the rail, and the port meet the fastest-growing county in the region.
markets.intro: Nassau County is the last uncongested quadrant of the Jacksonville metro — a county with an Atlantic deepwater port, two interstate exits, three federal highways, and a population growing faster than anywhere else on the First Coast. Commercial demand here runs on three engines. The SR-200 corridor between I-95 and Amelia Island is absorbing retail, medical, and service inventory as Yulee's rooftops multiply around Wildlight and the East Nassau employment center. The island economy — tourism, hospitality, marine, and the professional offices that serve it — keeps Fernandina Beach inventory scarce and tightly held. And the county's western reach along US-1 and US-301 through Callahan carries the industrial story: rail-served land, truck routes, and the large-parcel sites that no longer exist inside Jacksonville. Inventory is thin, deals are relationship-driven, and the public data undercounts what actually trades. That is exactly why a dedicated local commercial practice matters here more than in a downtown tower market.

faqs.q: What does commercial land cost in Nassau County?
faqs.a: It ranges widely by corridor: SR-200 retail frontage near I-95 commands the county's top land pricing, while US-1 and US-301 acreage west of the interstate still trades at a fraction of Jacksonville equivalents. Most transactions are unlisted or quietly marketed, so corridor comps matter more than portal searches.

faqs.q: Which Nassau County submarket is growing fastest?
faqs.a: The SR-200/A1A corridor through Yulee, anchored by the Wildlight master-planned community and the new employment centers around it. Retail pads, medical office, and flex space there lease ahead of delivery.

faqs.q: Is there industrial space in Nassau County?
faqs.a: Yes, but it is scarce and mostly owner-occupied. The supply story is land: rail-adjacent sites around Callahan and US-301, and yard-heavy parcels along US-17 minutes from I-95. Most industrial requirements here are solved by building, not leasing.

markets.name: Fernandina Beach
markets.tagline: A working port, a historic downtown, and the tightest commercial inventory in Northeast Florida.
markets.intro: Fernandina Beach is a fifty-block Victorian downtown attached to a working deepwater port, wrapped in an island economy that runs twelve months a year. Commercial property here behaves unlike anywhere else on the First Coast: buildings hold for generations, the historic district caps new supply by design, and buyers routinely wait years for a Centre Street address to surface. The corridors tell the story. Centre Street and its side blocks carry retail, restaurants, galleries, and the second-floor offices above them. Eighth Street — the A1A spine every islander drives daily — is where freestanding buildings, banks, and service retail concentrate. Sadler Road serves the beach side and the grocery-anchored daily-needs trade. And the 14th Street district around Baptist Medical Center Nassau has quietly become the island's medical-office submarket. When something trades here, it trades on relationships and preparation — knowing the zoning, the parking math, and the design-review process before the offer, not after.

faqs.q: How tight is commercial inventory in Fernandina Beach?
faqs.a: Extremely. The historic district is effectively built out, so availability comes from tenant turnover and estate sales rather than new construction. Well-priced downtown buildings often trade before they are publicly marketed.

faqs.q: What should I know before buying in the historic district?
faqs.a: Exterior changes and signage go through historic design review, parking requirements are satisfied differently than in suburban zoning, and many buildings pre-date modern code. None of it is prohibitive — but it should all be priced in before you offer.

faqs.q: Where is the medical office market on the island?
faqs.a: Clustered around Baptist Medical Center Nassau on S 14th and 18th Streets. Purpose-built clinical space rarely lists; most practices secure space through direct approaches to owners.

markets.name: Yulee
markets.tagline: The SR-200 corridor: where Nassau County's growth actually lands.
markets.intro: Yulee is where the county's population growth converts into commercial absorption. The nine miles of SR-200 between I-95 and the Amelia River have shifted in a decade from rural highway to the county's primary retail corridor — grocery anchors, national outparcels, medical clinics, and the service businesses that follow rooftops. Behind the corridor, the Wildlight master-planned community and the East Nassau Stewardship District are delivering the housing and employment base that underwrites the next decade of demand. The commercial logic here is simple and unforgiving: traffic counts, median cuts, and signal position decide retail value; I-95 proximity decides industrial and flex value along US-17; and entitled land in the path of the corridor appreciates faster than any improved asset in the county. Sites with full access and utilities are already scarce. For operators priced out of the island and investors who want growth-market fundamentals with Florida coastal demographics, Yulee is the working answer.

faqs.q: What are traffic counts on SR-200?
faqs.a: The corridor carries some of the heaviest volumes in the county, concentrated between I-95 and the bridge to the island. Every listing on this site cites its FDOT count with the station and year, so you can underwrite from the same figure the state publishes.

Wildlight's commercial parcels are released in phases by the master developer, and the surrounding SR-200 corridor trades independently. Both paths are viable depending on your use, timeline, and appetite for design guidelines.

faqs.q: Where does flex and light industrial go in Yulee?
faqs.a: Along US-17 and the side roads off SR-200 near I-95 — small-bay flex, contractor yards, and clear-span warehouses minutes from the interchange. It is the county's most practical logistics position short of building in Jacksonville.

markets.name: Callahan
markets.tagline: Rail, truck routes, and the large parcels the rest of the metro ran out of.
markets.intro: Callahan is Nassau County's working crossroads — the junction where US-1, US-301, and the CSX mainline meet twenty minutes from Jacksonville International Airport. For a century that geography made it a timber and agriculture town; the same geography now makes it the county's industrial land bank. Large, high-and-dry parcels with rail adjacency and federal-highway frontage exist here at a scale and price Jacksonville's industrial market abandoned years ago, and the county's certified mega-site program has put the area on the radar of manufacturers and logistics users hunting the Southeast. The town itself carries a steady retail and service trade serving western Nassau's fast-growing residential base, with US-1 frontage as the main street of that economy. The commercial play in Callahan is patience and position: corridor land ahead of the next rezoning cycle, rail-served sites ahead of the next industrial announcement, and small-town retail that gets stronger with every subdivision approved west of I-95.

faqs.q: Why do industrial users look at Callahan?
faqs.a: Scale and rail. Contiguous acreage on or near the CSX mainline, with US-301 and US-1 truck routes and the airport twenty minutes away, at land prices Jacksonville's industrial corridors left behind.

Western Nassau's residential growth is filling in the trade area, and US-1 through town is its main street. Daily-needs retail, quick service, and auto-oriented uses perform; destination retail still belongs on SR-200.

faqs.q: What about utilities on rural parcels?
faqs.a: It varies parcel by parcel — some corridor sites have water and sewer at the road, many run on well and septic. Utility due diligence leads every land conversation here, and it is the first thing worth verifying before contract.

markets.name: Amelia Island
markets.tagline: A resort island's commercial market: hospitality-grade demand, island-grade scarcity.
markets.intro: Amelia Island runs a two-sided commercial economy. On one side sit the resorts — the Ritz-Carlton and Omni Amelia Island anchor a hospitality market that fills restaurants, spas, golf, and event venues with visitor spending across all four seasons. On the other side sits a real year-round community of thirteen thousand islanders whose services — medical, professional, marine, food and beverage — occupy nearly every commercially zoned foot the island has. The result is structural scarcity: thirteen miles of barrier island, most of it residential, conservation, or resort-held, with commercial nodes at Sadler Road, the A1A corridor south toward the Plantation, and Fletcher along the beach. Assets here rarely reach open marketing, values hold through cycles that bruise mainland markets, and hospitality-adjacent uses pay a premium for any position inside the visitor flow. Buying or leasing on the island is less a search problem than an access problem — knowing who owns what, and being first in line when circumstances change.

faqs.q: Can I buy hospitality property on Amelia Island?
faqs.a: Occasionally — inns, restaurant buildings, and event venues do trade, but quietly and infrequently. Most opportunities move through direct relationships before they are ever publicly listed, which is why representation with island-specific reach matters.

faqs.q: What does retail lease for on the island?
faqs.a: Island retail carries a scarcity premium over the SR-200 corridor, with the strongest rates in the visitor-flow nodes near the beach and downtown. Exact comps shift with so few data points, so current corridor guidance beats any published average.

faqs.q: Is short-term rental or multifamily investment viable here?
faqs.a: Both exist under real regulatory boundaries — zoning and municipal rules govern where short-term rental operates, and multifamily sites are genuinely rare. The viable path is usually an existing asset reposition rather than ground-up development.
